title: Kernel Signer: SLA-driven Kernel Plan & Runtime Verifier
creator: Aisha Chen
description:
Problem: We need a deterministic, low-overhead way to choose and enforce kernel execution plans per-request that respect customer SLAs (latency tails and cost budgets) across heterogeneous hardware and variable sequence lengths. Current heuristic switching sometimes violates p99 latency targets during mixed bursts and when sequence-length distributions shift.

Proposal overview: Introduce a compact 'kernel signer' abstraction: an off-line synthesizer that generates small, verifiable kernel plans (signatures) for a given model+quantization+arch+seq-bucket. At runtime, a lightweight verifier quickly checks the signer and attaches a confidence score. The runtime then (a) prefers signed plans when the request's SLA budget is tight, (b) hedges with safe fallbacks when confidence is low, and (c) records telemetry for online re-synthesis. This ties kernel selection to an explicit SLA policy (latency budget and cost weight) instead of only raw latency estimates.

Key components and behavior: 1) Synthesizer (offline): simulated-annealer style search that composes kernel candidates, evaluates cost/latency via microbenchmarks and per-arch models, and emits a compact signature: a fingerprint, plan id, estimated latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), resource footprint, and a risk token. 2) Runtime verifier: verifies signature authenticity (signed by our autotune service) and checks estimated tail risk against the incoming request's SLA metadata. Adds verifier confidence score to routing decision. 3) Hedging policy: when verifier confidence < threshold or predicted p99 > SLA, runtime can: a) fallback to pre-tested safe kernel (higher cost, lower variance), b) start a hedged second execution on alternate kernel (speculative decode), or c) route to dedicated capacity tier. 4) Feedback loop: telemetry of signers that under/overestimate tails are fed back to the synthesizer for re-synthesis with adjusted cost models and safety margins.

Why different from existing work: Instead of purely online bandit or latency-estimator-based switching, this attaches a signed provenance artifact to kernel plans so routing decisions can be auditable, repeatable, and parameterized by explicit SLA policies per-customer. It reduces runtime exploration overhead and provides a clear rollback channel: unsigned or stale signatures are rejected.

Success criteria / acceptance: - p99 latency reduction for SLA-bound customers during mixed-burst tests (target: p99 improvement >= 20% vs baseline heuristic) - No >1% increase in token cost for non-SLA customers - Signer verification latency < 150 microseconds median on CPU path - False-accept rate of signatures < 0.1% in synthetic tamper tests

Links and artifacts: - Design doc (Confluence): https://redwood.atl/confluence/display/INF/Kernel+Signer+Design - Microbenchmark results (Drive): https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/kernel-signer/initial-bench - Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1148 - Dashboard prototype (Datadog): https://app.datadog.com/dash/kernel-signer-experiments

Open questions and trade-offs: - Signing overhead vs. freshness: how frequently should signers be regenerated for a model when workload seqlen drift is observed? (Current plan: regenerate on stable drift >10% p95 change or weekly). - Complexity: added offline step increases pipeline complexity. Mitigation: start with a limited set of hot models and seq-buckets (top 10 customer models). - Security: signatures must be tamper-resistant; we will use our existing KMS signing keys and compact signature blobs.

Rollout plan: 1) Implement synthesizer + signer storage service (staging) and offline batch synth for 5 hot models (2 weeks) 2) Runtime verifier added behind a feature flag; route 5% traffic for two pilot customers with SLA profiles (2 weeks) 3) Expand to 25% traffic and start adaptive re-synthesis if telemetry indicates underestimation (2 weeks) 4) Full rollout to SLA lane with monitoring and auto-fallback (1 sprint)

Monitoring and observability: new dashboards for signed-plan hit rate, verifier confidence distribution, signed vs fallback p50/p95/p99, signer freshness, and re-synthesis queue lag. Alerts for p99 regressions and signature verification spikes.

QA and testing: microbench harness for per-arch signer validation, chaos tests for mixed bursts (prefill-heavy and decode-heavy), and canary check for cost regressions. Unit tests for signature parsing/verifier, integration test with routing policy engine.

Notes: This ticket focuses on design + prototype synthesizer + runtime verifier. Followups for integration with rollout policies, auto-re-synthesis triggers, and per-customer risk budgeting live in sibling tickets.
updates: 2025-02-15: Ticket created by Aisha Chen. Draft design and list of components. Assigned to Marco.

2025-02-18: Spike complete: basic synthesizer can enumerate kernel plans for 4 kernels and produce latency p95 estimates within 12% of lab microbenchmarks. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1148

2025-02-21: Design review with PM and SRE. PM (Lina Park) requested explicit per-customer risk budget. SRE (Ravi Patel) requested signature expiry and replay protections. Action: add risk token and expiry fields to signature format.

2025-02-23: Prototype verifier added to runtime under flag 'kernel_signer_v1'. Local benchmarks show <120us median verification on x86 CPU path. Pushed initial metrics to Datadog dashboard (see Design doc).
2025-02-26: Decision: start pilot with two customers (ACCT-102 and ACCT-231) with strict SLA lane. Created dashboard and alert runbook. Next: schedule batch synthesis for their top 3 models.
2025-02-28: Blocker noted: synthesizer requires updated kernel microbench harness for chiplet topologies. Assigned to ENG-61804 to extend microbench (see dependencies).
